The Company is formulating a detailed plan for disposal / consumption of these inventories. 

Considering the market volatility, steel market dynamics, possibility of future additions to steel and pellet making capacity in the country which may augment the demand of these materials, the carrying value of the non-current inventories need not be adjusted for any unforeseeable changes in the future prices. Accordingly, in view of the management, the carrying values of the aforementioned inventories are the best estimates basis the information available at this stage. 

49.11  The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) had approved the in-principle strategic disinvestment of three SAIL units—Alloy Steels Plant (ASP), Durgapur; Visvesvaraya Iron & Steel Plant (VISP), Bhadravati; and Salem Steel Plant (SSP), Salem—on 27 th October 2016. Following this, the SAIL Board endorsed the decision in its 9 th February 2017 Board meeting and initiated the disinvestment process. The entire process of Strategic Disinvestment is being overseen by an Inter-Ministerial Group (IMG). The IMG is chaired by Secretary, Department of Public Assets Management (DIPAM) and co-chaired by Secretary (Steel). The Group appointed various Advisors to carry out the process. Despite two attempts for ASP, the process could not progress further due to either non-eligible or no bidders. SAIL is exploring options for performance improvement of ASP. 

For VISP, the EOI issued on 4 th July 2019 was annulled by IMG due to lack of bidder interest. The Alternative Mechanism (AM), based on recommendations from the Core Group of Secretaries on Disinvestment (CGD), has approved the annulment of EOI, initiation of process for closure of VISP, monetisation of its land preferably through the National Land Management Agency (National Land Monetization Corporation). SAIL Board in its 496 th meeting held on 16 th January 2023, has in-principle approved the proposal for the same. 

In the case of SSP, the EOI issued on 4 th July 2019 was similarly annulled as per DIPAM’s letter dated 5 th January 2024 due to lack of interest from shortlisted bidders. The SAIL Board approved this annulment in its 509 th meeting held on 12 th February 2024. 

In view of the current status and the various other processes which are underway, no adjustment in these financial statements is considered necessary at this stage.

50.1  DEFINED BENEFIT SCHEMES 

50.1.1 General Description of Defined Benefit Schemes: Gratuity : Payable on separation @15 days pay for each completed year of service to eligible employees who render continuous service of 5 year or more (for service beyond 30 year, one month’s salary for every completed year of service beyond 30 year). Maximum amount of ` 20 lakhs for executives & non-executives joined on or after 1st July, 2014. For non-executive employees joined before 1 st July, 2014, the gratuity accrued on pre revised Basic Pay and DA, as on the date of implementation of wage revision i.e. 18.10.2021 or ` 20 lakhs whichever is higher has been considered for actuarial valuation. 

Leave Encashment : Payable on superannuation to eligible employees who have accumulated Earned and Half Pay Leave, subject to maximum limit of 300 days combined for earned leave and half pay leave. Encashment of accumulated earned leave also allowed upto 30 days once in the Financial Year. 

Provident Fund : 12% of Basic Pay Plus Dearness Allowance, contributed to the Provident Fund Trusts by the company. 

Post Retirement Medical Benefits : Available to retired employees at company’s hospitals and/or under the health insurance policy. 

Post Retirement Settlement Benefits : Payable to retiring employees for settlement at their home town. 

Long term service Award : Payable in kind on rendering minimum 25 year of service and also on superannuation.

INDEPENDENT AUDITOR’S REPORT To the Members of Steel Authority of India Limited Comments Management’s Replies Report on the Audit of the Standalone Financial Statements Qualified Opinion 

1.  We have audited the accompanying standalone financial statements of Steel Authority of India Limited (‘the Company’), which comprise the Balance Sheet as at 31 March 2025, the Statement of Profit and Loss (including Other Comprehensive Income), the Statement of Cash Flow and the Statement of Changes in Equity for the year then ended, and notes to the standalone financial statements, including material accounting policy information and other explanatory information, in which are included the returns for the year ended on that date audited by the branch auditors of the Company’s branches/units/marketing regions as listed in Appendix 1. 2.  In our opinion and to the best of our information and according to the explanations given to us, and based on the consideration of the reports of the branch auditors as referred to in paragraph 17 below, except for the effects of the matters described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section of our report, the aforesaid standalone financial statements give the information required by the Companies Act, 2013 (‘the Act’) in the manner so required and give a true and fair view in conformity with the Indian Accounting Standards (‘Ind AS’) specified under section 133 of the Act read with the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015 and other accounting principles generally accepted in India, of the state of affairs of the Company as at 31 March 2025, and its profit (including other comprehensive income), its cash flows and the changes in equity for the year ended on that date. 

Basis for Qualified Opinion 

3 a) As referred in note 47.2 (a) to the accompanying standalone financial statements, the constitutional validity of the Entry Tax Act has been upheld by the Hon’ble Supreme Court and the matters relating to levy of entry tax are now pending before Regular Benches of the High Court. Pending decision by the Hon’ble High Court of Jharkhand, the management is of the view that no adjustment is required in the accompanying standalone financial statements of the Company for the disputed entry tax demand in Jharkhand state amounting to ₹ 105.13 crore as on 31 March 2025. However, in the absence of sufficient appropriate evidence to support the management’s view, we are of the opinion that a provision for entry tax liability should be recognised in the standalone financial statements. The Nine Judge Bench of the Hon’ble Supreme court, vide its order dated 11 th November, 2016, upheld the Constitutional validity of the Entry Tax legislations passed by the various States. However, the Bench directed that certain other matters raised by the Petitioner, such as matter relating to Entry Tax amounting to ₹105.13 crore on goods entering into the local area of Jharkhand from other States, etc. may be determined by regular benches hearing the matters. However, pending decision by the Courts, the disputed Entry Tax liabilities of ₹105.13 crore have been treated by the Company as Contingent Liability. Intelligent Steel Making the Future Green 158 

Comments Management’s Replies 

3 b) As referred in Note 47.2 (b) to the accompanying standalone financial statements, the Company has accounted for ₹344.75 crore refundable by Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) pursuant to the tariff order of Jharkhand State Electricity Regulatory Commission (JSERC) dated 10 th December, 2024, which follows the directions of the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL). The refund which is to be adjusted in 24 equal monthly instalments in the power bills has commenced from January 2025. As per the communication from DVC, the total refund amount of ₹344.75 crore includes ₹175.82 crore towards principal and ₹168.93 crore towards interest. Management is of the view that APTEL has still not issued final orders, as such JSERC tariff orders may still be subject to change due to the outcome of ongoing legal case pending before APTEL. However, the Company has adjusted the entire refund amount, including interest, against the total advance amount appearing in the books. This is not in compliance with the requirements of Ind AS 109, which require application of the Effective Interest Method and recognition of interest income separately in the Standalone Statement of Profit and Loss. 

The Company continues to carry an amount of ₹448.03 crore (₹216.87 crore shown in Other Current Asset, ₹132.09 crore shown in Other Current Financial Asset and ₹99.07 crore shown in Other Non-Current Financial Asset) as advance paid to DVC for the period from FY 2012–13 to FY 2016–17. The said amount is not under any legal or regulatory dispute, and management has not provided sufficient appropriate audit evidence demonstrating the basis for its continued recoverability. In our opinion, the amount should have been provided for in the standalone financial statements for the year ended 31 st March, 2025. Had the aforesaid matters been appropriately accounted for, the interest component embedded in the refund instalments would have been recognized as income as per Ind AS 109, resulting in a lower loss and higher equity for the year. Further, advances aggregating ₹448.03 crore should have been provided for, which would have resulted in a decrease in current assets, an increase in the loss, and a corresponding reduction in equity as at 31 st March, 2025. 

Impact of all the above qualifications on the accompanying standalone financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025 is as under: 

Particulars As at 31 st March 2025 Reported balances Balances after impact of all the qualifications which are quantified 

Other Equity 51,525.88 50,972.72 Deferred Tax Liability 6,422.33 6,283.11 Other Non Current Financial Assets 622.47 523.40 Other Current Financial Assets 1,221.31 1,089.22 Other Current Assets 2,910.94 2,694.07 Other Current Liabilities 4196.07 4,301.20 The Company’s view is that the cases are sub-judice and pending for adjudication before the various judicial authorities for a long time. Further, the civil appeal filed by DVC pertaining to tariff of 2004-09 against the Order of the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL), have been dismissed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India vide its Order dated 3 rd December, 2018. Accordingly, State Electricity Regulatory Commission (SERC) will finalise the retail tariff as directed by APTEL, the financial implication of which can only be ascertained after the Tariff fixation by SERC. Jharkhand SERC (JSERC) finalised the Category-wise Retail Supply Tariff of DVC for the period from FY 2006-07 to FY 2011-12 vide order dated 31 st October, 2023. However, DVC has preferred an appeal before Hon’ble APTEL against the order of the JSERC regarding the consideration of non-tariff income in totality in the tariff order. APTEL vide its order dated 5th February, 2024 allowed the appeal of DVC with request to the Commission to pass an order afresh at the earliest. The Commission in light of the Order of Hon’ble APTEL, passed the remand Order dated 23.07.2024. DVC challenged it before the Hon’ble APTEL regarding incorrect treatment of non-tariff income by JSERC in its tariff order. Hon’ble APTEL vide its interim order dated 15 th Oct 2024 stayed the impugned tariff and JSERC was directed to calculate category wise tariff for the period under consideration. SAIL filed Civil Appeals before the Supreme Court, against this interim order of Hon’ble APTEL, however, Supreme Court vide its order dated 27 th Jan. 2025 stated that it was not inclined to interfere with the impugned judgment passed by the Appellate Tribunal. In line with direction of Hon’ble APTEL, the JSERC has re-computed the ARR and category-wise tariff for the period FY 2006-07 to FY 2011-12 and issued the tariff order dated 10 th Dec. 2024. Annexure II Independent Auditor’s Report on the internal financial controls with reference to the standalone financial statements under Clause (i) of Sub-section 3 of Section 143 of the Companies Act, 2013 (‘the Act’) Comments Management’s Replies 

1.  In conjunction with our audit of the standalone financial statements of Steel Authority of India Limited (‘the Company’) as at and for the year ended 31 March 2025, we have audited the internal financial controls with reference to financial statements of the Company as at that date. 

Responsibilities of Management and Those Charged with Governance for Internal Financial Controls 

2.  The Company’s Board of Directors is responsible for establishing and maintaining internal financial controls based on the internal financial controls with reference to financial statements criteria established by the Company considering the essential components of internal control stated in the Guidance Note on Audit of Internal Financial Controls over Financial Reporting issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India. These responsibilities include the design, implementation and maintenance of adequate internal financial controls that were operating effectively for ensuring the orderly and efficient conduct of the Company’s business, including adherence to the Company’s policies, the safeguarding of its assets, the prevention and detection of frauds and errors, the accuracy and completeness of the accounting records, and the timely preparation of reliable financial information, as required under the Act. 

Auditor’s Responsibility for the Audit of the Internal Financial Controls with Reference to Financial Statements 

3.  Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the Company’s internal financial controls with reference to financial statements based on our audit. We conducted our audit in accordance with the Standards on Auditing issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (‘ICAI’) prescribed under Section 143(10) of the Act, to the extent applicable to an audit of internal financial controls with reference to financial statements, and the Guidance Note on Audit of Internal Financial Controls Over Financial Reporting (‘the Guidance Note’) issued by the ICAI. Those Standards and the Guidance Note require that we comply with ethical requirements and plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements were established and maintained and if such controls operated effectively in all material respects. 4.  Our audit involves performing procedures to obtain audit evidence about the adequacy of the internal financial controls with reference to financial statements and their operating effectiveness. Our audit of internal financial controls with reference to financial statements includes obtaining an understanding of such internal financial controls, assessing the risk that a material weakness exists, and testing and evaluating the design and operating effectiveness of internal control based on the assessed risk. The procedures selected depend on the auditor’s judgement, including the assessment of the risks of material misstatement of the financial statements, whether due to fraud or error. 5.  We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained and the audit evidence obtained by the branch auditors in terms of their reports referred to in the Other matter paragraph below, is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our audit opinion on the Company’s internal financial controls with reference to financial statements. Appropriate action has already been taken in this regard. ANNUAL REPORT 

2024-25 183 

Comments Management’s Replies Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to Financial Statements 

6.  A company’s internal financial controls with reference to financial statements is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A company’s internal financial controls with reference to financial statements include those policies and procedures that 

(i)  pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of the assets of the company; 

(ii)  provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the company are being made only in accordance with authorisations of management and directors of the company; and 

(iii)  provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorised acquisition, use, or disposition of the company’s assets that could have a material effect on the financial statements. 

Inherent Limitations of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to Financial Statements 

7.  Because of the inherent limitations of internal financial controls with reference to financial statements, including the possibility of collusion or improper management override of controls, material misstatements due to error or fraud may occur and not be detected. Also, projections of any evaluation of the internal financial controls with reference to financial statements to future periods are subject to the risk that the internal financial controls with reference to financial statements may become inadequate because of changes in conditions, or that the degree of compliance with the policies or procedures may deteriorate. 

Opinion 

8.  In our opinion, the Company has, in all material respects, adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements and such controls were operating effectively as at 31 st March 2025, based on the internal financial controls with reference to financial statements criteria established by the Company considering the essential components of internal control stated in the Guidance Note on Audit of Internal Financial Controls over Financial Reporting issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India.

MANAGEMENT’S REPLIES TO THE COMMENTS OF THE COMPTROLLER AND AUDITOR GENERAL OF INDIA UNDER SECTION 143(6)(b) OF THE COMPANIES ACT, 2013 ON THE STANDALONE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS OF STEEL AUTHORITY OF INDIA LIMITED FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 MARCH 2025 

The preparation of Financial Statements of Steel Authority of India Limited for the year ended 31 st March 2025 in accordance with the financial reporting framework prescribed under the Companies Act, 2013 (Act) is the responsibility of the management of the company. The Statutory Auditors appointed by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India under Section 139(5) of the Act are responsible for expressing opinion on the financial statements under Section 143 of the Act based on independent audit in accordance with the standards on auditing prescribed under Section 143(10) of the Act. This is stated to have been done by them vide their Audit Report dated 28 th May 2025. I, on behalf of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, have conducted a supplementary audit under Section 143(6) (a) of the Act of the Financial Statements of Steel Authority of India Limited for the year ended 31 st March 2025. This supplementary audit has been carried out independently without access to the working papers of the Statutory Auditors and is limited primarily to inquiries of the Statutory Auditors and company personnel and a selective examination of some of the accounting records. Based on my supplementary audit, I would like to highlight the following significant matters under Section 143(6)(b) of the Act which have come to my attention and which in my view are necessary for enabling a better understanding of the financial statements and the related Audit Report. 

COMMENTS MANAGEMENT’S REPLIES A COMMENTS ON FINANCIAL POSITION BALANCE SHEET (i) Non-current Assets Note: 4 - Property, Plant and Equipment: ₹ 65022.90 crore 

Principal Chief Conservator of Forest, Wildlife & Chief Wildlife Warden Jharkhand sanctioned (15 April 2025) Site - specific & Biodiversity Conservation Plan in compliance of the conditions laid by MoEF&CC towards environmental clearance of Jhillingburu-II, Gua Ore Mines of SAIL. As per approved plan, ₹69.93 crore (₹20.51 crore relating to 2024-25) was sanctioned for 10 years from 2024-25 to 2033-34. Plan for safe passage of elephants relating to Gua mines submitted by SAIL was sanctioned with a condition to deposit ₹27.58 crore (₹9.30 crore pertaining to 2024-25) in CAMPA account for 10 years from 2024-25 to 2033-34. Ind AS 116 stipulates that the lessee shall depreciate the right-of-use asset from the commencement date to the earlier of the end of the useful life of the right-of-use asset or the end of the lease term. Since, the above two plans specified that the expenditure to be incurred over 10 years from 2024-25 to 2033-34, management should have recognized the liability for entire amount and thereafter, year wise expenditure was required to be charged in line with the provisions of Ind AS 116 which was not done. This has resulted in understatement of mining rights by ₹97.51 crore and Provisions by ₹67.70 crore and understatement of Other Expenses and overstatement of Profit for the year by ₹29.81 crore. With regard to observation raised by audit, the demand to deposit the amount has been received from Divisional Forest Officer (DFO), Saranda on 18/06/2025 after the adoption of the accounts of the Company for the F.Y 2024-25 and hence could not be considered in FY 2024-25 However, necessary accounting for FY 2024-25 and Q1 of FY 2025-26 have already been done in Q1 of FY 2025-26 ii. Note 31 - Other Financial Liabilities: ₹ 9649.37 cror eThe above does not include ₹20.81 crore recovered in excess by SAIL/Bhilai Steel Plant from a contractor during 2014-15 to 2024-25 towards supply of water. Bhilai Steel Plant supplied water to a contractor for industrial use as per the contract (March 2010) for installation of Oxygen Plants. It was mutually agreed (December 2007) between BSP and the contractor to include requirement of water at 120 CuM/Hr. However, in the contract, water requirement was indicated as 240 CuM/Hr. Bhilai Steel Plant had been recovering water charges from the contractor at 240 CuM/Hr basis and reducing its water expenses by the same amount. The matter raised by the audit is a commercial matter and the party was selected on L-1 basis through open tender and the said matter is a part of contract agreement. This disputed case is pending before Hon’ble High Court of Chhattisgarh. Intelligent Steel Making the Future Green 188 

The contractor disputed the recovery and Arbitration Award (24 December 2018) was passed against SAIL and SAIL was directed to refund the excess amount recovered along with interest at 12 per cent till the date of refund. The decision was upheld (1 October 2019) by the Commercial Court (District Level), Raipur. The matter is pending before High Court. SAIL therefore has a present obligation as the issue involves interpretation of a clause of the Contract and the award of the Arbitral Tribunal, that was upheld by the Commercial Court. Also, it is probable that an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits will be required to settle the obligation and a reliable estimate of the obligation can be made. Thus all the criteria of Para 14 of Ind AS 37 is met and a provision should have been made. This has resulted in understatement of other financial liabilities (current) and overstatement of Profit by ₹ 20.81 crore. Based on the judgement of the Hon’ble High Court, necessary action will be taken. In FY 2025-26, the matter will be review again based on the instant observation of audit for necessary accounting. 

B COMMENTS ON PROFITABILITY i. Note 41: Other Expenses ₹ 29288.26 crore Note 47.1: Contingent Liabilities: ₹ 40112.29 crore 

SAIL operates iron ore captive mines in the State of Jharkhand (erstwhile Bihar), Odisha and Chhattisgarh for which royalty is paid. State government notified different legislations for levy of additional tax on the mineral which was challenged by SAIL. High Court of Bihar and Odisha ordered in favour of the Company against which respective State Government filed an appeal in Supreme Court of India. In case of Chhattisgarh, High Court ordered (1 October 2019) that no separate or parallel adjudication does require to be made in these cases and the issue, once decided by the Apex Court, will be applicable to all concerned. Audit noted that the Constitution Bench of Supreme Court of India in its judgement (24 July 2024) stated that royalty is not a tax and upheld State Governments decision to collect additional tax on minerals from 1 April 2005. SAIL has filed a counter affidavit with the regular bench of Supreme Court to whom the case was referred to by the Constitution bench. Audit observed that decision of Supreme Court has determined the applicability of the State Acts for the mineral excavated from 1 April 2005. SAIL has estimated a liability of ₹ 2687 crore (Jharkhand - ₹ 831 crore, Odisha- ₹ 1856 crore) where it did not receive any demand from State Government as the matter is pending in division Bench of Supreme Court of India. Since, nine-judge Constitution bench of Supreme Court of India has decided in favour of State Governments there is a possible obligation that Company will have to pay the demand. As such ₹ 2687 crore pertaining to Jharkhand and Odisha should have been disclosed in Contingent Liability as per para 10 of Ind AS 37 which was not done. In the State of Odisha, Hon’ble High Court in its judgement dated 5.12.2005 struck down the said Act and Rules framed thereunder. In the State of Jharkhand, Hon’ble High Court by its final Judgment dated 22.03.1999 held that Section 89 of the Act and Rules framed there under are ultravires and quashed section 89 & Rules thereunder. Hon’ble Constitution Bench (Nine Judges) of Hon’ble Supreme Court by Judgment dated 25.07.2024 ordered that the State Legislature has legal competence to frame such laws. However, many issues not addressed by Hon’ble Constitution Bench (Nine Judges) of Hon’ble Supreme Court pertaining to individual State Legislation have been referred back to the Regular Bench. The Orissa Rural Infrastructure and Social Economic Development Act, 2004 and Section 89 of Bihar (now Jharkhand) Coal Mining Area Development Act, 1992 are yet to be restored in the respective States by the regular bench of Supreme Court. SAIL has submitted a counter affidavit in Regular Bench of Hon’ble Supreme Court. Hence, at this stage it is not even possible to ascertain the applicability of Act as well as working out any figure. Also there is no demand from the states. Therefore, no disclosure is required under contingent liability in respect of additional mineral tax for the State of Odisha and Jharkhand. ANNUAL REPORT 

2024-25 189 

In case of Chhattisgarh, Company paid ₹ 256.47 crore (as on 31 March 2025) under protest and accounted for as Deposit with State Government and disclosed the amount as Contingent Liability. In view of the order of the High Court of Chhattisgarh of October 2019, that issue, once decided by the Apex Court, will be applicable to all concerned, in line with the provisions of para 14 of Ind AS 37 the amount should have been charged to expenditure. Non-accountal of the above has resulted in understatement of Other Expenses and overstatement of Profit by ₹ 256.47 crore and understatement of Contingent Liability by ₹ 2687 crore. Further, the above matter was also not reported by the Statutory Auditors in their Independent Auditors’ Report. 

In the State of Chhattisgarh, mentioned amount is paid under protest against demand from State Government which is sub-judice in the regular bench of Hon’ble Supreme Court as mentioned above. Therefore, the same is appearing under Contingent Liability. However, the observation of audit will be reviewed and necessary action, if required will be taken in FY 2025-26 based on further development in this regard. 

C COMMENTS ON DISCLOSURE 

(i) SAIL operated Jitpur underground colliery at 0.70 million tonne per annum and having mineable reserve of 21 million tonne and extractable coal reserve of 10.85 million tonnes as on 31 March 2025. Abnormal water seepage was noted in Jitpur colliery on 19 April 2024. Director General of Mines and Safety directed SAIL not to deploy any manpower for operation due to continuous seepage in colliery and the production was stopped from 23 April 2024. Central Institute of Mining and Fuel Research appointed by SAIL recommended (November 2024) for closure of colliery. The colliery has been closed, and SAIL has lost 10.85 million tonne of extractable reserve of coking coal. As the event has a material impact on the operational status of a unit, Company should have disclosed the fact as a separate disclosure in compliance to Para 17 of Ind AS 1 which was not done. The notes were deficient to that extent. Necessary disclosure will be done in accounts of FY 2025-26

Corporate Governance is the system of Policies, Rules, Procedures, Processes and Practices by which a company is administered, directed or controlled with the ultimate objective of maximising the value for all the stakeholders viz. Government, Investors, Shareholders, Customers, Vendors, Employees, Environment and the Society at large. As good governance measure being integral to a company, the concerned officers of the Company are accountable to its Stakeholders in terms of transparency, fairness, ethics and professional approach followed in the decisions taken by them. 

(a)  Company’s Philosophy 

The philosophy of the Company in relation to Corporate Governance is to ensure transparency, disclosures and reporting that confirms fully to laws, regulations, guidelines including DPE guidelines and robust policies formulated over the years and to promote ethical conduct throughout the Organization, with the primary objective of enhancing shareholders value, while being a responsible corporate citizen. Your Company is committed to confirming to the highest standards of Corporate Governance in the Country. It recognizes that the Board is accountable to all shareholders and that each member of the Board owes his/her first duty for protecting and furthering the interest of the Company. 

(b)  Board of Directors 

The Board of Directors being at the core of our Corporate Governance is entrusted with the responsibility of Management, Direction, Performance of the Company and ensuring that the long term interest of the stakeholders is protected and stakeholders’ value enhanced. The Board reviews and approves management’s strategic plans and business objectives and monitors the Company’s strategic direction. The Board of Directors functions in accordance with the powers delegated under the Companies Act, 2013, SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, Articles of Association, Corporate Governance Guidelines issued by DPE and other guidelines issued by the Government of India from time to time, as applicable to the Company. 

Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL) is a Government Company within the meaning of Section 2(45) of the Companies Act, 2013. In terms of the provisions of the Articles of Association of the Company, the strength of the Board shall not be less than six Directors or more than twenty four Directors. As per the Articles of Association, the power to appoint Directors vests with the President of India. Consequent to restructuring of the Board, vide letter no.3(4)/2007-SAIL (PC)(Pt) dated 25 th September, 2020, Government of India (GoI), Ministry of Steel (MoS) has conveyed the sanctioned strength of the Board of Directors as under: 

(i)  Nine Functional Directors including the Chairman & Managing Director and four Director In-charges for Integrated Steel Plants; 

(ii)  Two Government Nominee Directors; and 

(iii)  Eleven Independent Directors as per the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015.

During the FY 2024-25, none of the Directors were Members in more than 10 committees or Chairperson in more than 5 committees in all the listed entities where they were Directors. Further, during the year under review, there was no instance where the Board had not accepted any recommendation of any Board Sub-committee. Further, there are no inter-se relationships among the Directors on the Board.

(c)  Audit Committee: 

(i)  Terms of Reference: 

The terms of reference of Audit Committee of SAIL Board in line with the Regulation 18(3) read with Part C of Schedule-II of SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, include: the primary function to assist the Board of Directors in fulfilling its oversight responsibilities by reviewing the Financial Reports; the Company’s systems of internal financial controls and Risk management systems, Accounting and Legal compliance that Management and the Board have established; review Related Party Transactions in accordance with the Related Party Transaction Policy of the Company; and the Company’s Auditing, Accounting and Financial Reporting process generally. 

The Audit Committee reviews the reports of the Internal Auditors, meets Statutory Auditors and Cost Auditors, reviews the Auditors’ independence, performance and effectiveness of the audit process, discusses their findings, suggestions and other related matters and reviews Accounting Policies adopted by the Company. The Audit Committee reviews with the Management, the Quarterly and Annual Standalone and Consolidated Financial Statements and the Auditors’ Report thereon, before their submission to the Board. 

The minutes of the Audit Committee meetings are submitted to the Board, discussed, and taken note of. 

(ii)  Composition:

(d)  Nomination & Remuneration Committee 

(i)  SAIL, being a Government Company, the nomination and fixation of terms & conditions for appointment of its Directors, are made by the Government of India. However, the Company has constituted a Nomination & Remuneration Committee (NRC), the terms of reference of which, inter-alia, include to look into various HR issues, matters prescribed under the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI Regulations; to finalise Performance Related Pay (PRP) for the executives of the Company in terms of Department of Public Enterprises Guidelines on Corporate Governance for Central Public Sector Enterprises; etc. 

As on 31 st March, 2025, the Nomination &Remuneration Committee comprised of Prof.(Dr.) K. Jayaprasad, Independent Director (Chairman); Shri Amarendu Prakash, Chairman, SAIL; Shri Abhijit Narendra, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Steel (Government Nominee Director); as Members. As per Section 178(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC) shall identify persons who are qualified to become directors and who may be appointed in senior management in accordance with the criteria laid down, recommend to the Board their appointment and removal and shall specify the manner for effective evaluation of performance of the Board, its committees and individual directors. The evaluation is to be carried out either by the Board, NRC or by an independent external agency and NRC shall review the implementation and compliance of the evaluation system. Further, Regulation 17(10) & 25(4) of SEBI (LODR) 2015 and the Code for Independent Directors pursuant to Section 149(8) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires the performance evaluation of Independent Directors to decide their continuance or otherwise. The Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) has vide its Notification dated 5th June, 2015 notified exemptions to Government Companies from certain provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 which, inter-alia, provides that Sub Sections (2), (3) & (4) of Section 178 regarding appointment, performance evaluation and remuneration shall not apply to Directors of Government Companies. The appointment of Functional Directors as well as Part Time Non-Official Directors (Independent Directors) on the Board of SAIL is made based on nomination/appointment by Government of India (GOI). The terms & conditions of appointment as well as tenure of all Directors are also decided by GOI and there is a well laid down procedure for evaluation of Functional Directors and CMD by the Administrative Ministry. Further, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs vide Notification dated 5 th July, 2017 has notified amendments in Schedule IV of the Companies Act, 2013 relating to Code for Independent Directors, wherein, the clauses relating to evaluation of performance of Non-Independent Directors, Chairperson and Board have been exempted for Government Companies.

The appointment may, however, be terminated by either side on three months’ notice or on payment of three months’ salary in lieu thereof.

(f )  Risk Management Committee: The Company has constituted the SAIL Risk Management Committee (SRMC) in line with the Regulations of SEBI and the Chief Risk Officer of the Company is acting as the Secretary to the Committee. Chairman, Audit Committee, is the Chairman of the SRMC and the members comprise Directors on the Board of the Company. SAIL has adopted a comprehensive Risk Management Policy, which is available on the website of the Company- https://sail.co.in/sites/default/files/ Comp_policies/2020-02/ermpolicy.pdf. The Policy is designed to ensure timely risk identification, evaluation, and mitigation in a dynamic business environment. The SRMC is responsible for overseeing the Company’s risk management framework. Its key responsibilities include: Establishing a Structured Risk Management System; Formulating, Adopting, and Implementing the Risk Management Policy; Setting Standards for Risk Documentation; Reviewing the Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework for continued relevance and effectiveness; and ANNUAL REPORT

(xxv)  Risk w.r.t. Commodities: Pursuance to Circular No. SEBI/HO/CFD/CMD1/CIR/P/2018/ 0000000141 dated 15 th November, 2018, SAIL does not perceive any risk with respect to commodities, as it has taken adequate steps to ensure uninterrupted supply of major materials. However, in case of imported coking coal, there is a risk of interruption in supply as there are limited number of vendors and bulk supply from one geographical area. Action is being taken to increase vendor base through EOI route and increase coal basket by exploring new coal producing countries from different geographies like Russia, Mozambique, etc. For iron ore, SAIL has its own captive iron ore mines which meet its requirement. Similarly, for refractories and ferro-alloys, SAIL has its own captive Plants and SAIL is procuring limestone under Long Term Agreement. ANNUAL REPORT

(xxxii)  Foreign Exchange Risk and Hedging Activities: SAIL adopts a cautious and proactive approach for monitoring currency fluctuations and employing hedging strategies to safeguard itself from any adverse impact and to ensure stable, prudent treasury operations aligned with evolving global conditions. SAIL has a well-defined, Foreign Exchange Risk Management (FERM) Policy duly approved by the Board of Directors to address risks mainly from significant USD-denominated financial transactions, most of which relate to import of coking coal. As per the said Policy, coal exposures generally remain un-hedged, though hedging up to 25% may be undertaken based on recommendations of the Forex Risk Management Committee (FRMC), considering market conditions and expert inputs from banks. While short-term Buyer’s Credit Usage is currently ‘Nil’, foreign currency loans for future CAPEX/ MODEX activities may be fully hedged for their entire tenure to mitigate risks and lock in interest arbitrage, as per FERM Policy. Qualified opinion 

7.  Based on the procedures performed by us and to the best of our information and according to the explanations provided to us, in our opinion, the Company has complied, in all material respects, with the conditions of Corporate Governance as stipulated in the Listing Regulations and DPE Guidelines during the year ended 31 st March 2025, except to the following: 

a.  During the period from 08 th April, 2024 to 31 st March, 2025 there was absence of minimum number of Non-Executive Directors and One independent woman director in composition of Board as required under Regulation 17(1)(a) of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 as well as the number of Functional Directors on the Board was exceeding 50% of the actual strength as required under Para 3.1.2 of DPE Guidelines on Corporate Governance for CPSE’s. Further, there was absence of minimum number of Independent Directors during the period from 1 st April 2024 to 31 st March 2025 as required under Regulation 17(1)(b) of SEBI (LODR), Regulations, 2015 and Para 3.1.4 of DPE Guidelines on Corporate Governance for CPSE’s.

1 Water Use and Recycling Opportunity Water is a vital resource in steel manufacturing. Efficient water use not only ensures regulatory compliance but also reduces operational costs and enhances long-term sustainability. SAIL is actively pursuing “Zero Liquid Discharge” (ZLD) across all integrated steel plants. This involves deploying advanced effluent treatment technologies and water recycling systems. These efforts reduce freshwater dependency, lower effluent discharge costs, and improve environmental performance, which can attract sustainability-linked financing and improve investor confidence. Positive 2. Waste Management (Slag, Dust, Plastics) Opportunity Industrial waste, if managed effectively, can be transformed into valuable resources. Recycling slag, dust, and plastics reduces environmental impact and creates economic value SAIL has implemented systems to segregate, reuse, and monetize waste. BF Slag is used in cement manufacturing, dust is recycled in sinter plants, and plastics are handled through authorized recyclers. These practices reduce landfill costs, generate revenue from byproduct sales, and contribute to circular economy goals, enhancing SAIL’s ESG profile. 3 Greenhouse Gas Emissions & Carbon Footprint Opportunity Reducing emissions aligns with global climate goals and enhances SAIL’s competitiveness in green steel markets. It also opens doors to carbon credits, green bonds, and sustainability-linked incentives. SAIL is actively advancing its decarbonization agenda across integrated steel plants through key technological interventions such as CDQ, TRT, CDI, and Waste Heat Recovery systems to enhance energy efficiency and reduce fossil fuel dependence. The deployment of walking beam reheating furnaces is optimizing rolling mill operations. On the renewable energy front, SAIL aims to scale its capacity to 384 MW by FY 2028–29, transition to LED lighting, and pilot green hydrogen in steelmaking. R&D efforts are focused on CCUS, low-carbon technologies in collaboration with IITs, and slag utilization to curb indirect emissions. These initiatives are guided by a phased decarbonization roadmap, participation in the PAT scheme, and alignment with the National Green Hydrogen Mission—underscoring SAIL’s commitment to sustainable steel production and national climate objectives. Positive 4 Occupational Health & Safety Risk Ensuring the health and safety of employees is critical to maintaining uninterrupted operations, reducing liability, and complying with legal standards. Workplace incidents can lead to downtime, reputational damage, and financial penalties. SAIL has adopted the ISO 45001:2018 Occupational Health and Safety Management System across all plants. Regular internal and external audits, safety drills, and training programs are conducted. A dedicated Board Sub-Committee on Health, Safety & Environment monitors performance quarterly, driving continuous improvement and accountability. Despite the implementation of robust safety protocols, SAIL remains exposed to the risk of workplace accidents, which can result in operational disruptions, legal liabilities, and financial penalties. Positive 6 Human Rights Risk With a large and diverse workforce across multiple states, any lapse in human rights compliance can result in reputational damage, legal consequences, and loss of stakeholder trust. SAIL strictly adheres to ILO conventions and national labor laws. SAIL ensures fair wages, safe working conditions, and equal opportunities. Grievance redressal mechanisms are in place at multiple levels, allowing employees to report concerns confidentially. Regular training and audits reinforce ethical practices and compliance. Lapses in human rights compliance can result in regulatory fines and penalties for labor law violations, while operational costs may increase due to work stoppages, protests, or employee unrest. SAIL aims to lower specific PM emissions from 0.81 kg/tcs in 2015–16 to 0.56 kg/tcs by 2025–26, aligning with global best practices and national environmental standards. 

• SAIL is committed to enhancing sustainability, cost efficiency, and regulatory compliance by reducing 

specific water consumption in its integrated steel plants. SAIL aims to lower water usage from 3.83 m³/tcs in 2015–16 to 2.85 m³/tcs by 2025–26 through strategic interventions and best practices. 

• SAIL is committed to reducing CO 2 emissions in its integrated steel plants as part of its sustainability strategy and alignment with India’s climate goals. SAIL aims to lower specific CO 2 emissions from 2.60 T/tcs in 2015– 16 to below 2.302 T/tcs by 2030, with an interim target of 2.41 T/tcs by 2025–26. SAIL is also working toward achieving net-zero emissions by 2070, in line with national commitments.

Consumption (SEC) in its integrated steel plants to enhance operational efficiency, lower production costs, and meet sustainability objectives. SAIL targets a 9% reduction from the 2015–16 baseline of 6.51 Gcal/tcs, aiming to reach 6.08 Gcal/tcs by 2025–26.

Description This section is aimed at helping businesses demonstrate the structures, policies and processes put in place towards adopting the NGRBC Principles and Core Elements. S. No. Disclosure Question P1 P2 P3 P4 P5 P6 P7 P8 P9 Policy and management processes 6 Performance of the entity against the specific commitments, goals and targets along-with reasons in case the same are not met. 

• Details of performance of the entity against the specific commitments, goals and targets for 24-25 is given under the Principle 6. 

• Action plan for PM reduction: SAIL is implementing a comprehensive strategy to reduce particulate matter (PM) emissions across its integrated steel plants. This includes upgrading pollution control systems by installing advanced electrostatic precipitators (ESPs), bag filters, wet scrubbers, and dry fog systems. Process optimization measures such as Top Pressure Recovery Turbines (TRT), Coal Dust Injection (CDI), and Coke Dry Quenching (CDQ) are being adopted to minimize emissions. Infrastructure modernization involves commissioning taller coke oven batteries with CDQ and waste heat recovery, along with cleaner reheating furnaces. Material handling is being improved by enclosing conveyors and automating operations to reduce dust. Real-time monitoring is ensured through Continuous Emission Monitoring Systems (CEMS) integrated with a centralized MIS for compliance and audits. SAIL is also focusing on 100% utilization of blast furnace and BOF slag in construction applications to reduce dust from stockpiles. Green belt development is being expanded with native species to enhance dust capture and biodiversity. Employee engagement is promoted through regular environmental training and sustainability initiatives. Additionally, SAIL has partnered with BHP to explore innovative, low-emission steelmaking technologies using hydrogen and biochar, supporting long-term decarbonization and PM reduction goals. 

• Action plan for reduction in water consumption: SAIL is advancing a robust water conservation strategy to reduce specific water consumption in its integrated steel plants. The approach centers on maximizing water recycling through closed-loop systems, reverse osmosis, and membrane bioreactors, along with cascading water use across processes. Traditional cooling systems are being replaced with evaporative towers and air-cooled exchangers, while dry quenching and high-efficiency descaling are cutting water use at the source. Smart sensors, flow meters, and regular audits ensure real-time monitoring and rapid leak detection. Rainwater harvesting and groundwater recharge structures are being scaled across facilities. Employee awareness programs promote conservation culture, while R&D collaborations with IITs and CSIR are piloting low-water steelmaking and alternative cooling technologies. These efforts support SAIL’s broader goals of sustainability, cost efficiency, and zero-liquid discharge. 

• Action plan for reducing CO 2 emission: SAIL is pursuing an aggressive decarbonization strategy to reduce CO₂ emissions in its integrated steel plants. Key technological upgrades include CDQ, TRT, CDI, WHR systems, all aimed at improving energy efficiency and cutting fossil fuel use. Walking beam reheating furnaces are being deployed to optimize rolling mill operations. On the renewable front, SAIL is expanding RE to 384 MW by 2028–29, transitioning to LED lighting, and piloting green hydrogen for steelmaking. R&D efforts focus on Carbon Capture, Utilization & Storage (CCUS), low-carbon technologies in collaboration with IITs, and slag utilization to reduce indirect emissions. These initiatives are backed by a phased decarbonization roadmap, active participation in the PAT scheme, and alignment with the National Green Hydrogen Mission—reinforcing SAIL’s commitment to sustainable steel production and India’s climate goals. • Action plan for reducing energy consumption: SAIL is actively working to reduce SEC through a multi-pronged strategy focused on technology, optimization, and innovation. Key process improvements include CDQ, TRT, CDI, WHR systems, all aimed at minimizing energy loss and maximizing reuse. Walking beam reheating furnaces are being adopted for their superior efficiency in rolling mills. Energy recycling is enhanced through gas recovery systems and real-time Energy Management Systems (EMS), while load balancing helps reduce peak demand. SAIL is also integrating renewable energy, targeting 384 MW of capacity by 2028–29, and deploying LED lighting with smart controls to cut auxiliary consumption. These efforts are supported by policy initiatives such as participation in the PAT scheme, alignment with the NMEEE, and regular corporate energy audits—reinforcing SAIL’s commitment to energy efficiency and climate goals.

8 Details of the highest authority responsible for implementation and oversight of the Business Responsibility policy / (ies). 

The Board is at the Apex of the Governance Framework at SAIL. The management of issues pertaining to economic, environmental and social areas are taken up by various Plants/ Units regularly. The Plant/Unit heads review and monitor the status reports in conjunction with the agenda papers. These reports are prepared with the valuable inputs provided by the respective departments/divisions, on the economic, environment and social performances including legal compliance and are regularly and methodically put up to the Board Sub Committees for examination, comments and recommendations. The input and observations of the Board Sub Committees are examined and analyzed by the top management. The Board is informed about these observations which subsequently helps in business decision making.

2.  a. Does the entity have procedures in place for sustainable sourcing? (Yes/No) b. If yes, what percentage of inputs were sourced sustainably? 

Yes, SAIL incorporates environmental, social, and governance (ESG) principles into its sourcing strategy for goods, services, and materials. The company prioritizes working with suppliers who are committed to sustainable practices and can demonstrate compliance with standards related to environmental stewardship, ethical labor practices, and social accountability. 

SAIL’s integrated steel plants (ISPs) procure essential raw materials like iron ore, limestone, and dolomite from its own captive mines. These mines are certified under Integrated Management Systems (IMS), including ISO 9001 for quality, ISO 14001 for environmental management, and ISO 45001 for occupational health and safety. Additionally, these mines have received star ratings from the Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM), reflecting their adherence to responsible mining standards. 

A substantial share of SAIL’s coking coal needs is fulfilled through imports from developed countries that follow stringent ESG guidelines and global sustainability standards. SAIL has also led the way in adopting ISO 14001-based Environmental Management Systems across its steel plants and storage facilities. 

3.  Describe the processes in place to safely reclaim your products for reusing, recycling, and disposing at the end of life, for (a) Plastics (including packaging) (b) E-waste (c) Hazardous waste and (d) other waste. 

Not applicable. 

Steel is highly recyclable and considered the world’s most recycled metal. Its durability and versatility allow widespread reuse and life extension. Its magnetic properties make it easy to separate from other materials for its recycling. It is genuinely cradle-to-cradle material, with end-of-life steel seen as an input rather than waste. Steel recycling is environmentally beneficial, conserving vital natural resources and reducing landfill waste. Recycling of steel is a sustainable practice that offers significant environmental and economic benefits, contributing to a more circular and resource-efficient economy. In FY 2024–25, over 1.41 million tonnes of scrap were effectively reused in the production cycle at SAIL Plants. ANNUAL REPORT

4.  Whether Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) is applicable to the entity’s activities (Yes / No). If yes, whether the waste collection plan is in line with the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) plan submitted to Pollution Control Boards? If not, provide steps taken to address the same. 

Yes. Under India’s Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016, Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) places the onus on producers, importers, and brand owners (PIBOs) to manage the entire lifecycle of their plastic packaging. This includes ensuring its recycling, reuse, or safe disposal. 

As an importer of plastic-packaged goods, SAIL has complied with these regulations by registering its plants on the Central Pollution Control Board’s (CPCB) centralized EPR portal and securing the necessary EPR certification.

10.  Health and safety management system: a.  Whether an occupational health and safety management system has been implemented by the entity? (Yes/ No). If yes, the coverage such system? 

Yes, SAIL has adopted a comprehensive Occupational Health and Safety Management System aimed at achieving the highest standards that not only comply with but exceed regulatory health and safety requirements. Most of SAIL’s Plants and Units are certified under ISO 45001:2018, with coverage aligned to system specifications. Intelligent Steel Making the Future Green 232 

In accordance with statutory norms, regulations, and internal policies, SAIL consistently works to prevent workplace-related illnesses and accidents. Health and safety are integral to all operational activities, supporting risk assessment and providing safeguards against potential hazards. Regular health check-ups and internal and surveillance audits are conducted to drive continuous improvement in safety practices, standards, and overall performance. 

Coverage of Occupational Health Infrastructure 

y Occupational Health Centres (OHCs), on-site dispensaries, and hospitals are available at Plants and Units, staffed by trained medical professionals. 

y Regular pre-employment and periodic health check-ups are conducted to monitor employee wellness. 

y Occupational surveillance programs are in place for early detection and prevention of work-related illnesses. 

y Specialised clinics, address specific occupational risks such as respiratory health, hearing conservation, and ergonomic stress. 

y Hygiene Survey covering the workplace conditions like temperature, dust level, etc are conducted 

y Emergency medical response systems, including ambulances and trauma care, are in place. 

y Health awareness initiatives focus on lifestyle management, stress reduction, and disease prevention. 

Salient Safety Management Practices 

y A robust framework for hazard identification, risk assessment, and accident prevention is operational. 

y Safety procedures are embedded in all operational processes and regularly reviewed. 

y Training and capacity-building programs are conducted for employees and contract workers on safe practices. 

y Behaviour Intervention programs like line walks by all executives including senior officers are conducted to transform safety culture 

y Regular internal and external safety audits are conducted to assess system effectiveness and ensure continual improvement. 

y Emergency preparedness drills, safety campaigns, and toolbox talks are held to reinforce a culture of safety. 

Integrated Approach 

Health and safety are treated as integral components of overall business sustainability. Cross-functional teams and committees oversee compliance, monitor performance, and drive improvements across the enterprise. This integrated approach ensures a proactive culture where employee well-being is prioritized, and workplace risks are effectively managed. 

b.  What are the processes used to identify work-related hazards and assess risks on a routine and non-routine basis by the entity? 

Yes, SAIL has established a comprehensive and well-structured Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA) procedure as part of its proactive safety management approach. This system is designed to systematically identify potential hazards, evaluate associated risks, and implement effective control measures to ensure a safe working environment. 

In addition to the standard HIRA process, SAIL employs a range of advanced tools and methodologies to strengthen its risk management framework, including: 

y Quantitative Risk Assessment (QRA) and HAZOP (Hazard and Operability) Studies – used for detailed analysis of complex processes and systems to identify potential failure points and operational risks. 

y Bow-Tie Analysis – a visual risk assessment method that helps in understanding the pathways from potential hazards to consequences, along with preventive and mitigative controls. 

y Regular Inspections and Audits – conducted to ensure compliance with safety standards and to identify areas for improvement. 

y Safety Observation and Behavioral Intervention Rounds – aimed at promoting a culture of safety through real-time feedback and corrective actions based on observed behaviors. 

y ROKO-TOKO Drives and Awareness Campaigns – internal initiatives designed to engage employees in safety practices, raise awareness, and reinforce safe behavior across all levels of the organization. 

These measures are part of SAIL’s broader commitment to fostering a safety-first culture, minimizing operational risks, and ensuring the well-being of its workforce. ANNUAL REPORT 

2024-25 233 

c.  Whether you have processes for workers to report the work-related hazards and to remove themselves from such risks. (Y/N) 

Yes, SAIL has a robust Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA) system in place that covers both routine and non-routine tasks. Based on these assessments, Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and Standard Maintenance Procedures (SMPs) are developed at the departmental level. Employees are regularly trained and made aware of key safety practices to ensure a strong safety culture. 

These procedures are periodically reviewed and updated, especially following any incident, to incorporate lessons learned and enhance preventive measures. SAIL also maintains a structured incident reporting and investigation mechanism to identify root causes and implement corrective actions. Recommendations from investigations are uniformly applied across all plants to prevent recurrence. To encourage proactive reporting, motivational schemes for reporting near-miss incidents are in place at both the plant and corporate levels. 

To further strengthen workplace safety, SAIL leverages digital platforms such as safety portals, WhatsApp groups, and mobile applications for real-time hazard and incident reporting. 

Additionally, under an ongoing safety management consultancy initiative, ‘Zero Tolerance Rules’ and ‘Life Saving Rules’ have been developed to discourage violations of safety norms by employees and contract workers, reinforcing accountability and compliance.

12.  Describe the measures taken by the entity to ensure a safe and healthy workplace. 

SAIL has implemented a comprehensive Safety Policy that prioritizes the well-being of its employees, contractors, and communities residing near its plants, units, and mines. Oversight of health, safety, and environmental matters is ensured through a dedicated Board Sub-Committee on Health, Safety & Environment (BSC on HSE), which regularly reviews related policies, systems, and procedures. 

At the corporate level, the SAIL Safety Organization (SSO) centrally monitors and supports safety initiatives across all operational sites. Safety performance is reviewed weekly at the highest level within each plant/unit, reflecting SAIL’s commitment to continuous improvement and risk mitigation. 

A structured and systematic approach to safety is adopted, involving hazard identification, risk assessment, and implementation of control measures to maintain risks at acceptable levels. Best practices from the steel industry, known as Good Safety Practices (G-SaPs), are actively identified and integrated into operations. Intelligent Steel Making the Future Green 234 

SAIL undertakes a wide range of initiatives to promote safe working conditions and enhance safety performance, including: 

y Occupational Health & Safety (OHS) Policy 

y Multi-level safety performance reviews (Board, Sub-Committee, Corporate, Plant) 

y Safety Committees for collaborative oversight 

y Compliance with statutory safety regulations 

y Safety training programs (induction, on-the-job, refresher, and LEO workshops) 

y Standard Operating and Maintenance Procedures (SOPs & SMPs) 

y Safety Talks and Toolbox Talks 

y Permit to Work and Protocol systems 

y Implementation of high-risk safety standards (e.g., work at height, confined space, electrical and gas safety, conveyor belt, rail and road safety) 

y Safe management of hazardous processes using tools like HAZOP and Bow-Tie analysis 

y Regular OHS audits and inspections 

y Theme-based safety drives and campaigns 

y Inspection and certification of tools, tackles, and equipment 

y Incident reporting, investigation, and root cause analysis 

y Emergency preparedness plans and mock drills 

y Use of digital platforms (web portals, mobile apps, WhatsApp groups) for real-time safety reporting 

y Safety promotion and motivational programs 

y Vehicle speed monitoring within plant premises for road safety 

y Industrial hygiene surveys (noise, dust, lighting) and periodic medical examinations 

To further strengthen its safety culture, SAIL has engaged reputed Safety Management Consultants for transformational initiatives at Bhilai, Rourkela, Bokaro, ISP Burnpur, and Durgapur Steel Plants. These efforts aim to elevate existing safety standards and embed a culture of safety excellence across the organization.

15.  Provide details of any corrective action taken or underway to address safety-related incidents (if any) and on significant risks / concerns arising from assessments of health & safety practices and working conditions. 

SAIL has implemented a range of corrective measures to address safety-related incidents and prevent their recurrence. These include: 

y Thorough investigation of all safety incidents, with key learnings shared across the organization to ensure consistent implementation of corrective actions. The effectiveness of these actions is verified during regular safety audits. 

y Review and revision of Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), Standard Maintenance Procedures (SMPs), and Safety Manuals in the specific area or function where the incident occurred, ensuring that updated protocols reflect lessons learned. ANNUAL REPORT 

2024-25 235 

y Use of Technology & AI o AI Tools for Analysis: Near Miss incidents analyzed using AI tools like ChatGPT, Meta AI, DeepSeek to prevent recurrence. o Digital Systems: Online systems to log unsafe conditions observed during Behavior Interventions (BI) and SEE (Safety Engagement & Encouragement) rounds. o Digital dashboards for incident reporting, investigation, and safety monitoring. 

y Training & Awareness Programs: Regular safety training, behavioral programs, workshops and mock drills to build awareness and strengthen safety culture. Digital tools and expert-led sessions like Suraksha Samvad support continuous learning and SOP development. 

y Application of the risk control hierarchy to mitigate significant health and safety risks identified during assessments. This includes: * Field Visits: To inspect safety preparedness and implementation of safety standards. Elimination of hazards where possible * Substitution with safer alternatives * Engineering controls, such as the use of technology and digital tools * Administrative controls, including safety training, supervision, visual alerts, and monitoring systems * Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) to safeguard workers when other controls are insufficient These measures reflect SAIL’s commitment to continuous improvement in workplace safety and proactive risk management.

3.  Provide details of instances of engagement with, and actions taken to, address the concerns of vulnerable/ marginalized stakeholder groups. 

SAIL’s plants have consistently undertaken initiatives to support the development of Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs) through the organization of Vendor Development Programs (VDPs). In addition, Special Vendor Development Programs (SVDPs) have been conducted with a focused objective of fostering an enabling ecosystem for SC/ST entrepreneurs. These programs were organized in collaboration with the National SC-ST Hub Office (NSSHO), with active participation from the Dalit Indian Chamber of Commerce & Industry (DICCI) and the Tribal Indian Chamber of Commerce & Industry (TICCI). During these sessions, participants were briefed on SAIL’s procurement processes, vendor registration procedures, and the specific provisions available for SC/ST and women-owned enterprises. 

These engagements also serve to inform vendors about SAIL’s procurement requirements, items earmarked for SC/ST and women vendors, and the benefits extended to MSEs from these communities. SAIL has also actively participated in various conclaves organized by National SC ST Hub Office (NSSHO) to further promote entrepreneurship among SC/ST groups. 

To enhance financial awareness, representatives from Invoice Mart are invited to select SVDPs to educate participants on the advantages of bill discounting through the Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS). In FY 2024–25, SAIL successfully conducted 56 VDPs and 27 SVDPs across its plants. 

Furthermore, SAIL plants provide ongoing support to local MSEs through mentoring, training, technical assistance, and capacity-building initiatives. To stimulate regional industrial development, SAIL also offers locally based MSMEs— particularly those situated in the same districts as its five Integrated Steel Plants (ISPs)—access to steel at competitive and affordable rates, supported by favorable commercial terms. 5.  Has the entity implemented a mechanism for Zero Liquid Discharge? If yes, provide details of its coverage and implementation. 

SAIL is taking significant strides toward achieving the ambitious goal of Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) at all its ISPs. By prioritizing the treatment and recycling of all wastewater within the plant boundaries, SAIL is reinforcing its commitment to environmental stewardship. Key achievements and ongoing efforts include: 

y Treatment and recirculation of approx. 128 million m³/year of wastewater across the ISPs. 

y Effluent treatment facilities with a total capacity of 500 m³/hour installed at Durgapur Steel Plant during FY 2024-25. 

y Storage capacity of the lagoon at Rourkela Steel Plant enhanced by 3 lakh m³ through de-silting. 

y All upcoming units within SAIL plants are envisioned to operate on the ZLD concept. 

To drive continuous improvement, SAIL is implementing several initiatives, including the adoption of advanced technologies, special measures to maximize reuse of treated effluents, and third-party assessments to identify further opportunities for optimization.

10.  Briefly describe the waste management practices adopted in your establishments. Describe the strategy adopted by your company to reduce usage of hazardous and toxic chemicals in your products and processes and the practices adopted to manage such wastes. 

SAIL’s integrated strategy combines innovation, compliance, and resource efficiency to manage industrial and hazardous waste responsibly, reduce reliance on harmful substances and drive progress toward a circular economy and sustainable industrial future. SAIL is committed in its Corporate Environment Policy to minimize source-wise solid waste generation and maximise its utilisation to the tune of 100%. The 4Rs principle — Reduce, Reuse, Recycle and Recover — is widely applied at SAIL plants, enabling significant contributions toward sustainability 

SAIL generates various by-products such as blast furnace (BF) slag, basic oxygen furnace (BOF) slag, mill scale, flue dust and refractory waste, etc. These by-products are not treated as waste but are transformed into valuable resources through innovative processes. For instance, molten BF is fully granulated for utilization in the cement industry. On the other hand, BOF slag is used mainly internally through recycling it in BF & steel melting shop as partial replacement of limestone and in sinter making as base-mix. Solid wastes like mill scale and lime/dolo fines are recycled entirely through sinter making process and waste refractory bricks are fully utilized through either selling to external agencies or reusing internally. 

Recognizing the untapped potential of BOF slag, SAIL is investing heavily in R&D to develop advanced waste management techniques. Collaborative initiatives with renowned research institutes have paved the way for innovative applications, such as: 

y Eco-Friendly Fertilizer Development: 

In partnership with ICAR-Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI) under the Ministry of Steel, SAIL is exploring usage of BOF slag in developing cost-effective fertilizers. Slag Based Value Added Products (SSBVAPs) have been developed by IARI and these SSBVAPs are undergoing field trials at all the five ISPs of SAIL, demonstrating their potential for sustainable agriculture and soil improvement Intelligent Steel Making the Future Green 248 

y Paver Blocks Manufacturing: 

Rourkela Steel Plant launched ‘Eco Brick’, an ecofriendly paver block manufacturing facility for utilizing BOF slag, to promote sustainability and waste utilization. The facility is equipped to produce high quality paver blocks with a concrete grade of M200 and a block thickness of 80 mm with a daily capacity of 1,000 blocks/day. 

Durgapur Steel Plant has set up a unit for manufacture of paver blocks by using weathered BOF slag (0-5mm size) in place of river sand. As a measure for increasing solid waste utilization, Salem Steel Plant has also started making paver blocks by utilizing its EAF slag through outsourced agency. 

This initiative significantly enhances slag utilization, reducing waste disposal challenges and supporting a circular economy in steel production. 

SAIL’s operations adhere to the Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016 and it is ensured that all hazardous waste is carefully inventoried, quantified, and either safely disposed of in captive secured landfills facility or through the authorized agencies. Wherever it is feasible, hazardous materials are reused/co-processed, thereby promoting circularity and reducing dependency on virgin resources. 

E-wastes and Battery waste are being disposed through authorized recyclers. Negligible quantity of construction & demolition waste is generated at some of the plants, which is internally utilized. During demolition/dismantling of specifically old structure/building, significant quantity of waste is generated which is disposed of through external agencies. 

The Company also adheres to the EPR in plastic waste management. All SAIL Plants are registered with the CPCB under the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016.

5.  Does the entity have a business continuity and disaster management plan? Give details in 100 words/ web link. 

SAIL units comply with all the safety and regulatory laws, ensuring a robust Business Continuity and Disaster Management Plan at both the corporate and the unit level. These plans developed with external expertise and approved by the Chief Inspector of Factories, address business uncertainties and safeguard the health and safety of workers and the public. 

Objectives of Disaster Management Plan: 

y Protect personnel inside and the public outside the plant 

y Rescue and provide medical treatment to the casualties 

y Safeguard plant, machinery, equipment, and other assets 

y Contain incidents and restore normal operations swiftly 

y To bring incident under control and ensure a rapid return to normal operation after emergency 

The plan covers both on-site and off-site emergencies. Regular mock drills are conducted to test the effectiveness of risk mitigation measures, and emergency resources, including a buffer stock of essential raw materials, are always maintained. Ongoing training and awareness programs are held to ensure preparedness. 

Regular audits by the National Safety Council validate our safety efforts. The plan includes risk assessments, emergency response strategies, and continuous employee training. We also maintain a resilient supply chain, strong communication protocols, and red undant systems to minimize disruptions, ensuring quick recovery from any emergency. 6. 3.  Describe the mechanisms to receive and redress grievances of the community. 

SAIL has a diverse and multi-dimensional approach to get feedback from the communities via holding regular community meetings, periodic interaction with municipalities and Town administrative committees and active engagement with the local society so as to understand if they have any views, issues, complaints and grievances related to the interventions. 

Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS) is an online platform available to the citizens 24x7 to lodge their grievances to the public authorities on any subject related to service delivery. CPGRAMS is also accessible to the citizens through standalone mobile application downloadable through Google Play store and mobile application integrated with UMANG. Intelligent Steel Making the Future Green 254 

The status of the grievance filed in CPGRAMS can be tracked with the unique registration ID provided at the time of registration of the complainant. CPGRAMS also provides appeal facility to the citizens if they are not satisfied with the resolution by the Grievance Officer. After closure of grievance if the complainant is not satisfied with the resolution, he/ she can provide feedback. If the rating is ‘Poor’ the option to file an appeal is enabled. The status of the Appeal can also be tracked by the petitioner with the grievance registration number. Issues which are not taken up for redress: 

y RTI Matters 

y Court related/Subjudice matters 

y Religious matters 

y Suggestions 

y Grievances of Government employees concerning their service matters including disciplinary proceedings etc.

PRINCIPLE 9: BUSINESSES SHOULD ENGAGE WITH AND PROVIDE VALUE TO THEIR CONSUMERS IN A RESPONSIBLE MANNER ESSENTIAL INDICATORS 1.  Describe the mechanisms in place to receive and respond to consumer complaints and feedback. 

Consumer Complaints: 

SAIL has established a robust mechanism to effectively handle customer grievances. Customers can file a Quality Complaint (QC), after which the concerned Branch Executive inspects the reported material. If needed, support from a regional Application Engineer (AE) or the relevant Plant is provided to assist and speed up the resolution process. If the complaint is found to be valid, a return order is processed, followed by a refund, reinforcing customer trust and satisfaction. 

Customer Feedback: 

To enhance customer interaction and accessibility, SAIL has introduced an AI-powered chatbot named ‘SAIL SARATHI’ that simplifies navigation and provides information to users. Additionally, SAIL operates a verified WhatsApp Business account, which is integrated with the SAIL SARATHI app for seamless communication. 

To further strengthen customer engagement, the Central Marketing Organization (CMO) has launched a dedicated app called “SAIL Grahak Sampark.” This app helps CMO executives efficiently plan, manage, and optimize customer meetings. ANNUAL REPORT
